claims.label: ψ gives probabilities
claims.summary: Born proposed in 1926 that, in collision processes, the wave function does not describe a spread-out particle but determines the probability of finding the particle — proportional, as he added in proof, to the square of the amplitude.
voice: In collision problems the wave does not describe where the particle's charge is spread. It tells us the probability of finding the particle — more precisely, as I added in proof, the square of the amplitude. The particles move according to laws of probability; the probability itself propagates in accordance with the law of causality.
The electron arrives whole, at one place. What the wave distributes is not the electron but the chance of finding it.
claims.reasoning: Scattered electrons are detected as whole particles at definite places; only the statistics of many events follow the wave.
evidence: Collision experiments: electrons are always detected as whole particles.
objections: Schrödinger: this abandons the physical reality of the wave.
Einstein: statistics may reflect an incomplete description.
claims.later: The Born rule is now standard. Born received the Nobel Prize for it only in 1954.

claims.label: Give up determinism — by choice
claims.summary: Born asked in 1926 whether any quantities could fix the outcome of an individual collision, answered that he saw none, and said he was inclined to give up determinism in the atomic world — while stating that this was a philosophical question physical arguments alone could not decide.
voice: I raised the question directly last year: is there any hope of finding quantities that would fix the outcome of an individual collision? I do not think so. I am inclined to give up determinism in the world of atoms. But I will be honest — that is a philosophical question, and physical arguments alone do not decide it.
claims.reasoning: No known quantity distinguishes one electron's fate from another's in identical conditions; but the absence of such quantities is not a proof they cannot exist.

claims.label: The theory agrees everywhere tested
claims.summary: As co-author of the joint report, Born endorsed the conclusion that quantum mechanics is a closed theory, supported by agreement with experiment wherever the statistical interpretation had been tested.
voice: Our report ends with a strong statement, and I stand by it: quantum mechanics is a closed theory. Wherever the statistical interpretation has been tested — in collisions, in spectra, in the intensities of lines — it agrees with experiment.
claims.reasoning: Empirical adequacy across the tested domain plus internal consistency.

claims.label: Probability refers to each case
claims.summary: By inference from his 1926 papers, Born would resist restricting ψ to ensembles: his collision probabilities refer to each individual scattering event.
voice: Einstein, I understand your first reading — it is where the statistical interpretation began. But our collision experiments are done one electron at a time, and the probability refers to each of them. To restrict the wave to ensembles is not a refutation of the theory; it is a decision not to say what the theory says.
claims.reasoning: The probability interpretation was introduced for single scattering events.
claims.later: The proceedings do not record a reply by Born to Einstein's two-viewpoint remark; this exchange is the simulation's inference.
